note.explanation: In a metal, outer electrons move freely among positive ions. These mobile electrons bind the ions together and help explain the properties of metals.
examples: Sodium releases one electron per atom, so its metallic bond is weaker than magnesium's.
Mobile electrons in a metal help it conduct heat and electricity.
note.checkAnswer: A metallic bond is positive metal ions bound together by mobile electrons.
note.simple: Think of positive metal ions surrounded by a shared pool of moving electrons. The shared electrons hold the ions together.
note.checkQuestion: What holds the positive ions together in a metallic bond?
note.title: Metallic Bond
steps: Metal atoms can lose their outer electrons easily.
The outer electrons move freely between the metal atoms.
The metal atoms become positive ions.
The positive ions are bound together by the mobile electrons.
note.answer: A metallic bond is a type of chemical bond in which positively charged ions are bound together by mobile electrons.

options: Mobile electrons move through the metal
The metal atoms form separate molecules
The metal ions remain fixed in one place with no electrons
The metal becomes a solution in water
mcqs.stem: Which feature of metallic bonding helps metals conduct electricity?
rationales: This is correct because mobile electrons can move through the metal and carry charge.
This is wrong because metallic solids are not made of separate molecules in this section's model.
This is wrong because mobile electrons are present and are not all fixed in place.
This is wrong because dissolving in water is not the reason metals conduct electricity.

options: Each sodium atom releases one electron
Each sodium atom releases two electrons

mcqs.stem: Why is the metallic bond in sodium described as not very strong?

This is wrong because the section says each sodium atom releases only one electron.
This is wrong because the section does not describe sodium bonding by gaining electrons from magnesium.
This is wrong because sodium does have mobile electrons in the metallic-bond model.

options: Magnesium releases two electrons per atom
Magnesium releases no electrons
Magnesium atoms form covalent molecules

mcqs.stem: Why is magnesium's metallic bond stronger than sodium's?
rationales: This is correct because each magnesium atom releases two electrons and becomes a two-positive ion.
This is wrong because magnesium releases two electrons according to the section.
This is wrong because the section explains magnesium using metallic bonding, not covalent molecules.
This is wrong because magnesium has two positive charges per ion, compared with sodium's one.

written.text: Give a comparison of metallic bond with an ionic bond.
written.finalAnswer: In a metallic bond, positively charged metal ions are bound together by mobile electrons. In an ionic bond, oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction.

written.text: Explain the properties of metals keeping in view the nature of metallic bond.
written.finalAnswer: Metals have lustre; they usually have high melting and boiling points, are good conductors of heat and electricity, and are usually hard and heavy. Mobile electrons make metals good conductors of heat and electricity. The atoms are strongly held and arranged in rows, making metals hard and heavy. When pressure is applied, upper rows slip past lower rows, changing the shape; metals can therefore be drawn into wires and sheets.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask what holds metal ions together: write that mobile electrons bind positively charged ions.
A constructed-response or descriptive question may ask how a metallic bond explains a property; state the particle feature and then connect it to the property.
For malleability and ductility, mention pressure and the upper rows slipping past the lower rows.
Use the sodium–magnesium comparison when asked how metallic-bond strength depends on the number of positive charges and mobile electrons.

yourTurn.question: Why is the metallic bond in magnesium stronger than that in sodium?
solution: Each sodium atom sets free only one electron.
Each magnesium atom releases two electrons to acquire two positive charges.
The metallic bond in magnesium is therefore stronger than that in sodium.
yourTurn.answer: Magnesium releases two electrons per atom and forms two-positive ions, so its metallic bond is stronger than sodium's.

steps.why: Sodium is the comparison metal in the section's example, and its atoms release one electron each.
steps.text: In sodium metal, each sodium atom sets free only one electron.

steps.why: The section says magnesium releases two electrons, giving its ions two positive charges.
steps.text: In magnesium metal, each magnesium atom releases two electrons to acquire two positive charges.

steps.why: The number of positive charges and mobile electrons affects the strength of a metallic bond.
steps.text: The metallic bond in magnesium metal is stronger than that in sodium metal.

steps.why: The section uses melting point as evidence of the stronger bond.
steps.text: Magnesium metal melts at a higher temperature than sodium metal.

example.question: Why does magnesium have a stronger metallic bond and a higher melting point than sodium?
example.answer: Magnesium releases two electrons per atom and acquires two positive charges, while sodium releases only one electron per atom. Magnesium therefore has a stronger metallic bond and melts at a higher temperature.

explain.title: The metallic bond
explain.body: A metallic bond, is therefore a type of chemical bond which has positively charged ions bound together by the mobile electrons. In a metal, the outer electrons move freely between spaces among atoms instead of staying attached to one particular nucleus.

explain.title: The strength of a metallic bond
explain.body: The strength of a metallic bond depends upon two factors: the number of positive charges present on the positive ions and the number of mobile electrons set free by each atom. Magnesium releases two electrons per atom, so its metallic bond is stronger than sodium's, where each atom sets free one electron.

explain.title: Conductivity
explain.body: The presence of freely moving electrons in metals makes them good conductor of heat and electricity. The mobile electrons can move through the metal.

explain.title: Hardness and changing shape
explain.body: In metals, the atoms are strongly held and arranged in the form of rows one above the other. This arrangement makes them hard and heavy. When pressure is applied, the upper rows of atoms slip pass the lower rows, changing the shape of the metal. Metals can therefore be drawn into wires and sheets.

mistakes: Do not say that the mobile electrons are attached to just one particular nucleus; the section describes them as moving freely among the atoms.
Do not confuse a metallic bond with an ionic bond: metallic bonding involves mobile electrons binding positive metal ions.
When comparing magnesium and sodium, include both the number of electrons released and the effect on bond strength.
For malleability and ductility, do not just write “metals bend”; explain that rows of atoms slip past one another under pressure.
